The measurement of deferred tax reflects the tax consequences that would follow from the manner in which the Company expects, at the reporting date, to recover or settle the carrying amount of its assets and liabilities. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset only if: a) the Company has a legally enforceable right to set off current tax assets against current tax liabilities; and b) The deferred tax assets and the deferred tax liabilities relate to income taxes levied by the same taxation authority on the same taxable entity. m) Employee benefits Short-term employee benefits Short-term employee benefits are measured on an undiscounted basis and are expensed as the related service is provided. A liability is recognised for the amount expected to be paid if the Company has a present legal or constructive obligation to pay this amount as a result of past service provided by the employee and the obligation can be estimated reliably. Defined contribution plans Obligations for contributions to defined contribution plans such as Provident Fund and Employee State Insurance Corporations are expensed as the related service is provided. Defined benefit plans The Company’s net obligation in respect of defined benefit plans is calculated separately for each plan by estimating the amount of future benefit that employees have earned in the current and prior periods, after discounting the same.

The calculation of defined benefit obligations is performed annually by an independent qualified actuary using the projected unit credit method. Re-measurement of the net defined benefit liability, which comprise actuarial gains and losses are recognised immediately in other comprehensive income (OCI). Re-measurement, if any, are not reclassified to the Standalone Statement of Profit and Loss in subsequent period. Net interest expense (income) on the net defined liability (assets) is computed by applying the discount rate, based on the market yield on government securities as at the reporting date, used to measure the net defined liability (asset). Net interest expense and other expenses related to defined benefit plans are recognised in the Standalone Statement of Profit and Loss. When the benefits of a plan are changed or when a plan is curtailed, the resulting change in benefit that relates to past service or the gain or loss on curtailment is recognised immediately in the Standalone Statement of Profit and Loss. The Company recognises gains and losses on the settlement of a defined benefit plan when the settlement occurs. Other long-term employee benefits The Company’s net obligation in respect of long-term employee benefits is the amount of future benefit that employees have earned in return for their service in the current and prior periods. They are therefore measured at the present value of expected future payments to be made in respect of services provided by the employees up to the end of the reporting period using the projected unit credit method. The discount rates used are based on the market yields on government securities as at the reporting date. Re-measurements are recognised in the Standalone Statement of Profit and Loss in the period in which they arise. Other long-term benefits include payable in respect of long-term incentive scheme recorded based on arithmetical model estimating the possible cash outflows based on assessment of parameters of the scheme and pro-rated to the completed service period and discounted at present value. n. Share-based payment transactions Employees Stock Options Plans (“ESOPs”) and Employee Stock Grant Scheme (“ESGS”): The grant date fair value of options granted to employees is recognised as an employee benefits expense, with a corresponding increase in equity, over the period that the employees become unconditionally entitled to the options. The expense is recorded for each separately vesting portion of the award as if the award was, in substance, multiple awards. The increase in equity recognised in connection with share-based payment transaction is presented as a separate component in equity under “Employee stock grant scheme reserve”. The amount recognised as an expense is adjusted to reflect the actual number of stock options that vest.

o) Borrowing costs Borrowing costs are interest and other costs that the Company incurs in connection with the borrowing of funds and is measured with reference to the effective interest rate applicable to the respective borrowing. Borrowing costs, pertaining to development of long-term projects, are transferred to Construction work-in-progress, as part of the cost of the projects till the time all the activities necessary to prepare these projects for its intended use or sale are complete. All other borrowing costs are recognised as an expense in the period in which they are incurred. p) Cash and cash equivalents Cash and cash equivalents in the balance sheet comprise cash at banks and on hand and short-term deposits with an original maturity of three months or less, which are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value. For the purpose of the Standalone Statement of Cash Flows, cash and cash equivalents consist of cash and short-term deposits, as defined above, net of outstanding bank overdrafts as they are considered an integral part of the Company’s cash management. q) Earnings per share Basic earnings per share is computed by dividing the profit / (loss) after tax by the weighted average number of equity shares outstanding during the year. Diluted earnings per share is computed by dividing the profit / (loss) after tax as adjusted for dividend, interest and other charges to expense or income (net of any attributable taxes) relating to the dilutive potential equity shares, by the weighted average number of equity shares considered for deriving basic earnings per share and the weighted average number of equity shares which could have been issued on conversion of all dilutive potential equity shares. If potential equity shares converted into equity shares increases the earnings per share, then they are treated as anti-dilutive and anti-dilutive earning per share is computed. r) Provisions and contingent liabilities A provision is recognised when the Company has a present legal or constructive obligation as a result of past events and it is probable that an outflow of resources will be required to settle the obligation in respect of which a reliable estimate can be made. Provisions (excluding retirement benefits) are discounted to their present value at a pre-tax rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the liability and are determined based on the best estimate required to settle the obligation at the balance sheet date. These are reviewed at each balance sheet date and adjusted to reflect the current best estimates. The unwinding of the discount is recognised as finance cost.

Beauty and Purpose

Every Lodha development is an invitation to experience rare luxury. We partner with the world’s finest architects and designers to set new benchmarks in luxury living, ensuring that each project enhances not just the skyline but also the lives of those who call it home.

We are guided by a deep appreciation for beauty - in form, in feeling and in function.

Our prestigious developments embody a rare confluence of craftsmanship, aesthetic elegance, unmatched service and elevated experiences. Creating spaces that cultivate kinship, we design homes and communities that foster well-being, celebrate aspirations and enrich lives in ways both tangible and profound; offering our patrons the gift of connection to themselves, to each other and to the world around them.

Lodha stands at the forefront of India’s premium real estate landscape, redefining urban living through thoughtfully designed residential and commercial developments. More than just spaces, our creations are meticulously crafted, nurturing environments that enrich lives through exemplary design, impeccable attention to detail and unparalleled service.

BRANDED, TIER-I RESIDENTIAL DEVELOPERS A PREFERRED CHOICE AMONGST HOMEBUYERS

India’s rapid urbanisation is driving a substantial increase in demand for quality urban housing. Driven by the pursuit of better employment opportunities and living conditions, a growing number of people are relocating to urban areas. The United Nations predicts that India’s urban population will surpass its rural population by 2050, signaling a sustained and enduring demand for real estate in urban and metropolitan areas.

The housing market has delivered overall stable growth, despite elevated mortgage rates after sharp increase in repo rate by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in FY23. Higher interest rates significantly reduced demand for entry-level and lower mid-income homes, the segments most affected by increased mortgage rates, with reduced loan eligibility requiring larger upfront payments. Change in policy stance and policy rate cuts by RBI are expected to stimulate demand in these segments. Income tax rate cut by the Central Government will further augment disposable income in the hands of homebuyers and support demand.

Over the past two decades, the perception of a home in a consumer’s mind has evolved from just being a necessity to a high value consumer product. Previous perceptions of a home being merely four walls and a roof caused consumers to overlook differences between good developers and not so good developers. Following a decade marked by project delays, budget overruns and quality issues, consumers are increasingly prioritising

established brands with a proven history of on-time, within budget and high-quality delivery.

Homes are now seen as status and source of lifestyle upgrade. Homebuyers, similar to consumers of other high-value products, seek the assurance of a reputed brand, which is synonymous with trust and reliability and prefer to buy from branded developers. Market share of listed and leading non-listed developers has doubled to 34% in FY24 from 17% in FY17 and will increase further as trend towards consolidation is expected to continue.

The size of Indian urban households has experienced a paradigm shift, with a growing preference for nuclear families over traditional joint families. This shift has resulted in increasing demand for residential properties, particularly in urban areas.

Execution capability is going to be an increasingly critical differentiator among branded developers. Our backward-integrated model with in-house construction capability provides us with a significant advantage. Nearly 50% of our 5,414 employees are dedicated to engineering, design and construction, helping us to deliver the world’s finest developments. This in-house expertise enhances operational agility and eliminates margin leakage to third-party contractors, driving robust profitability.

We have a clear and well-defined strategy of acquiring land parcels for project development with a balanced mix of outright land purchases and Joint Development Agreements (JDAs) with land owners. This approach enables us to strike a balance between leveraging the strength of our balance sheet to acquire new land, while also being conservative on debt. Our goal is to deliver quality products to our customers, achieve 20% pre-sales growth and a 20% return on equity and fully utilise our execution strength optimally without spreading ourselves too thin in the process. To achieve this, we use a balanced land acquisition strategy, combining outright purchases and JDAs which allows us to scale efficiently and deliver high-quality developments. In the steady state we aim to drive 40% of our pre-sales through JDA projects which are capital light in nature.

Having seen and experienced the excesses in the real estate sector in the last decade, we maintain a strict Net Debt to Equity ceiling of 0.5X. We intend to keep debt well below this ceiling, to ensure that debt becomes an enabler rather than being primary growth driver. Growth should and will be driven by a self-sustaining business model, with debt capped at the stated levels. Land acquisition will primarily be funded through operating cash generated by the development business and debt will be employed in an opportunistic manner for strategic expansion.

While residential real estate remains our core competency, we are strategically growing our annuity business in a calibrated manner, in order to de-risk our development activities. Our target is that by FY31, the annuity income should cover the interest expense of the development business and the fixed overheads of the Company. Our annuity income is derived from three key segments. First, the High Street retail, which we will continue to develop alongside select residential projects and select offices. Second, our digital infrastructure business, which serves the dual purpose of providing annuity income while also creating economic activity and providing employment. Third, from the facility management business, which already manages ~70,000 housing units. Over time, we intend to grow this business into a much larger business unit. We intend to focus on these three streams to generate annuity income and do not plan to undertake independent large-scale office or retail developments.

We aim to bring diversity in our product portfolio to help us generate consistent growth. We are the only developer with a presence across mid-income, premium and luxury segments with a wide range of price points starting from H 5 Mn to H 3 Bn. Our pre-sales for FY25 were driven by ~40 operating projects across diverse segments, cities and construction life stages. This project diversity, coupled with a strong sales infrastructure, ensures consistent and predictable pre-sales growth. Our presence across the three cities of MMR, Pune and Bengaluru has further provided diversity in consumer profiles. While MMR has given exposure to the consumers employed in BFSI, media and entertainment and corporate front offices, our diversification in Pune and Bengaluru has brought in consumers employed in manufacturing, IT services and startups. This extensive diversification coupled with our focus on sustenance sales ensures consistent pre-sales and shields us from market downturns across housing segments, locations and GDP sub-segments.

RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS

Committed to strong risk governance, our comprehensive risk management policy provides clear guidelines for managing risks across the organisation. This policy defines our risk appetite, establishes a robust framework with clear objectives and processes, fosters a risk-aware culture and enhances our competitive edge.

Recognising the fast-paced and evolving nature of the business environment, we proactively manage both opportunities and risks through our comprehensive Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework. Aligned with industry best practices, this structured approach ensures the systematic identification, assessment, mitigation and ongoing monitoring of risks across all our operations, with clear accountability and oversight mechanisms in place.

We regularly review and update our risk management processes to ensure their sustained relevance and effectiveness in addressing the spectrum of risks we encounter.

Ensuring quality and preventing errors upfront is a shared responsibility across all levels. Each operating department proactively manages risks as part of their routine activities. The Internal Risk Management Committee systematically reviews our operational functions and activities, commercial framework and technology platforms, ensuring a robust “Maker Checker” principle. The Internal Audit function provides independent assurance on the effectiveness of business operations and the risk management and oversight process. Internal Audit conducts regular reviews and its findings are presented to the Audit Committee on a quarterly basis.

PALAVA - A CITY OF REFINED LIVING

At Palava, refined living is not just a privilege, it is a way of life. Drawing inspiration from Singapore’s visionary urban planning, Palava embraces the acclaimed ‘5-10-15 minute principle’. Designed for seamless walkability, the city ensures that all essential experiences, from leisure and recreation to education and retail, are always a short stroll away. This innovative approach fosters a healthier, more active lifestyle while reducing vehicle dependency, creating cleaner air and a more serene, balanced environment for residents. A planned city where every space, amenity and detail is meticulously designed to elevate everyday moments into extraordinary experiences; from thoughtfully curated, climate-conscious residences to world-class recreational facilities, Palava sets a new standard for sophisticated urban living. Over a decade ago, Palava was envisioned as a solution to the urban chaos and liveability challenges prevalent in the island city of Mumbai. Palava demonstrates an economically viable model of high-quality, smart and sustainable urbanisation, enabled by meticulous planning, thoughtful design and exceptional service and governance. This forward-thinking urban model integrates eco-friendly practices at every level; from efficient building orientations to extensive green spaces and reflective materials that reduce heat absorption. The carefully designed city maximises natural ventilation and reduces heat retention. The strategically placed towers enhance airflow while naturally cool shaded courtyards offer respite from the heat. The orientation of the towers helps minimise internal heat gains on one side, while on the other, it aids in additionally shading tree-lined walkways.

Lush with over 32,000 trees of 200 species and a diverse array of shrubs, grasses, creepers and trees, Palava is as beautifully green as it is cool. The impact of Palava’s climate-conscious design is striking. A 2024 study done by the Lodha Net Zero Urban Accelerator highlights that Palava’s maximum land surface temperature is 3°C cooler than nearby Kalyan-Dombivli and 2°C lower than Mumbai.

Palava stands as India’s first integrated greenfield city, serving as a model for sustainable urbanisation. Designed to be a self-sufficient neighbourhood with easy access to retail, health and wellness, education, places of worship, transportation and even commercial spaces; at Palava, luxury goes beyond state-of-the-art facilities. Nearby, elegance and comfort define the Senior Citizen Office, a dedicated, thoughtfully designed space for the

We design buildings to achieve thermal comfort through passive design measures like efficient envelope and natural ventilation and daylight, reducing overall energy needs, which can help save up to 30% on electricity bills.

We prioritise materials that reduce carbon footprints, from greener concrete mixes, to recycled steel and more, we consistently advance circularity through our designs. We build with an impressive embodied carbon footprint and continue to work towards its reduction in line with our net zero goals.

Low-flow fixtures, rainwater harvesting and wastewater treatment systems are integrated, saving up to 50% of potable water across our projects.

Energy-efficient systems like 5-star rated air conditioners in homes and other leading-edge efficiency integrations in other systems also help keep the energy demand and cost down for our residents.

Solar rooftop plants are planned to power common areas and infrastructure loads contributing to the growing renewable energy share in our developments. We have close to 15MW of solar photovoltaic capacities operating or under development across our projects.

Developments are planned for walkability, with easy access to schools, healthcare and retail, reducing vehicle dependency and emissions.

As the first Indian real estate company with SBTi-validated net-zero targets, we aim for carbon neutrality by 2050. All our projects are green certified with the current certified portfolio exceeding 60 Mn Sq ft.

EXECUTION AND CONSTRUCTION

Energy-efficient Construction Practices Electricity used during construction almost entirely comes from renewable sources. We have been operationally carbon neutral since March 2024 and have been ramping the integration of renewable energy in our operations since 2019. We adopt energy-efficient techniques to minimise environmental impact during construction.

Water Management During Construction Water conservation is a priority on our construction sites. We use recycled water for activities like dust suppression, irrigation, flushing, etc. alongside efficient use of rain water, where available, for other construction activities.

Construction Waste Minimisation and Circular Use We minimise construction waste through careful planning and recycling, promoting a circular economy. Over 90% of construction waste at Lodha gets diverted from landfill and largely gets used or recycled through third party engagements.

GREEN AND OPEN SPACES

Greenery and Urban Planning

Our master planning prioritises integrating expansive green spaces—urban forests, gardens and playgrounds—within our developments. These landscapes enhance well-being, promote active lifestyles, foster a connection with nature and improve community biodiversity. Strategically placed green spaces and tree cover cool the urban environment, mitigating the heat island effect, shading walkways and reducing energy consumption. Integrating blue and green infrastructure further cools the micro-climate while improving energy and water management. Large open spaces increase rainwater percolation, enhancing groundwater recharge and limiting surface runoff. Multi-layered vegetation naturally filters dust and particulate pollution. By embedding nature-based solutions, we create resilient and sustainable communities prioritising environmental stewardship. Recognising the multifaceted benefits of greenery— ecological balance and social well being—we maximise its impact to foster vibrant, livable urban environments.

Our projects are designed as integrated ecosystems, offering residents a well-planned community where essential amenities such as schools, offices, clubhouses, sporting arenas, retail outlets and green spaces are within easy reach.

Net Positive Carbon Impact

The built environment contributes significantly to climate change, accounting for up to 40% of carbon emissions, with energy systems being the main driver. To address this, we follow a three pronged approach: improving material efficiency and reducing embodied carbon, enhancing energy performance and accelerating the transition to clean energy through renewable integration in buildings and enabling sustainable transport systems within and beyond our developments. Together, these efforts foster a more sustainable and low-carbon built environment.

Clean Energy Initiatives: Our commitment to clean energy is evident across our operations. Our construction sites and standing assets are powered entirely by renewable entirely by renewable energy, sourced through a combination of on-site and off-site generation and various available procurement models. This transition has led to a significant reduction in our Scope 1 and 2 emissions, decreasing by approximately 77% from the FY22 baseline as we shifted our electricity requirements to renewable sources.

The proportion of renewable energy in our total electricity consumption has nearly increased five-fold in last three years, underscoring our dedication to supporting India’s 2070 net-zero target.

Energy Efficiency Initiatives Passive Design: We prioritise passive design strategies to minimise energy demand by optimising building orientation, natural ventilation and daylight utilisation. Through sun path and wind analysis, we strategically position buildings to maximise natural light and reduce the need for air conditioning. Passive elements such as performance windows, shading and insulation further minimise heat gain and enhance thermal comfort. Utilising advanced software like Design Builder and Ansys, we conduct in-depth studies on ventilation, heat gain and shading to ensure buildings effectively leverage natural airflow and daylighting while minimising heat absorption, thereby reducing reliance on mechanical cooling systems. Active: Energy management is a continuous focus across our projects. We conduct regular energy audits to assess performance and identify improvement opportunities, driving progress towards our target of a 5% annual reduction in energy intensity leading to a EPI of <100kWh/ m2/year in each commercial building by

2030. Each audit results in a site-specific action plan, with energy consumption meticulously monitored before and after implementation to verify effectiveness. Our commitment is exemplified in our new office buildings, which operate significantly below the 125 kWh/sqm/yr energy performance index. This performance is driven by high-COP chillers, automated building management systems, premium efficiency motors, regenerative elevators and 100% LED lighting. With residential energy use accounting for approximately 57.3% of our total emissions, we integrate climate-responsive building designs, urban cooling solutions and high efficiency equipment in our developments. Recognising that air conditioners are major energy consumers, we mandate the installation of BEE 5-star rated units across most of our developments, achieving a 30% energy saving compared to 3-star models. We have installed 55,095 5-star AC units, delivering a cooling capacity of 65,895 tonnes—representing the highest penetration of energy-efficient <40 kWh/sqm/year

Embodied Carbon Reduction: We actively reduce embodied carbon through two key strategies; material efficient design, which optimises structures for performance with fewer resources and adoption of low-carbon alternatives including sustainable materials and circularity principles to minimise the overall carbon footprint in construction.

Our focus on efficient design and circular construction processes minimises waste and optimises material use. Recognising that purchased goods and services, particularly construction materials like cement, steel and aluminum, contribute approximately 40.1% of total lifecycle emissions in our product, we have conducted detailed benchmarking to assess the embodied carbon footprint of our buildings.

This analysis informs our targeted interventions and innovative solutions to reduce carbon intensity. Notably, last year completed a 23-story building using a triple-blend concrete mix (OPC, Fly Ash, GGBS), replacing 47% of traditional cement and achieving a 36.75% reduction in embodied carbon. This year we initiated a pilot for Limestone Calcined Clay Cement (LC3), in partnership with IIT-Delhi, which offers up to a 40% potential reduction in emissions compared to conventional cement, with full-scale implementation anticipated in coming years.

Low Flow Fixtures and Metering We are committed to reducing water consumption across our operations and developments. As part of this effort, we have set a target to limit water usage during construction to a maximum of 50 litres per square foot for all new projects. To support real-time monitoring and informed decision making, smart water metres are being installed at all active sites, enabling continuous tracking and data-driven reduction strategies. In our new developments, we integrate a suite of water conservation measures— including low-flow water fixtures, pressure reducing valves and water sub-metering systems. These features are implemented to enhance water efficiency, improve system maintenance and uptime, lower overall demand and advance our vision of building water positive communities.

Delivering Homes with Enhanced Indoor Air Quality Apartments handed over to residents are designed to prioritise superior indoor air quality, contributing to a healthier and more comfortable living environment. Adequate natural ventilation is provided through well-placed operable windows and design layouts that promote cross ventilation. CLEAN MOBILITY

Clean mobility forms a key pillar of our sustainable urban planning strategy, aimed at reducing transport-related emissions, alleviating congestion and enhancing the quality of life for residents.

By focusing on walkability, shared transportation and electrification, we are shaping communities that enable climate conscious, active and healthy lifestyles.

5

CLIMATE CHANGE

Climate change is reshaping the risk landscape, with increasing exposure to floods, cyclones, extreme heat and water scarcity—factors that can directly impact well-being, disrupt infrastructure and business continuity. Our approach is grounded in proactive resilience and design. We integrate climate adaptation and mitigation measures across planning and development, combining passive design strategies, energy-efficient systems, nature-based solutions and low carbon materials to reduce emissions and build climate-resilient assets.

6

We integrate forecasted climate data and regional risk insights into project design through internal tools and expert engagement, enabling developments to remain adaptive to changing climate conditions. Our property management teams are trained in emergency response protocols, providing an added layer of preparedness within our overall resilience strategy. Water resilience is a key focus. In addition to infrastructure solutions like rainwater harvesting and permeable surfaces, we support behavioural change through

awareness campaigns that promote efficient and responsible water use. As a leading real estate developer, we view environmental upgradation as core to sustainable urban development. From walkable, low-carbon neighborhoods to decarbonised construction and shared mobility systems, our climate strategy supports enhancing environmental outcomes, resilience and our net zero goals.

Walkability Our developments are designed with wide and shaded pedestrian pathways to ensure a safe and convenient walking experience. These features reduce reliance on vehicles for short distances, promote active living and contribute to lowering emissions at the community level. Our township projects are planned using the ‘5-10-15 principle’—daily needs and schools are placed within a 5-minute walk, recreational spaces within 10 minutes and essential services such as healthcare and offices within a travel distance of 15 minutes, thereby encouraging walkable, self-sustained neighborhoods.

Shared Transportation To support shared and low-carbon commuting, we integrate bicycle-sharing infrastructure in our township projects

and operate feeder buses within developments and up to nearby public transport hubs. These initiatives promote public transportation over private vehicles and encourage a shift toward more sustainable mobility

Electrification We are actively expanding Electric Vehicle (EV) infrastructure across all our developments to accelerate the transition to clean mobility. Through a strategic partnership with Tata Power, operating as a Charge Point Operator (CPO), EV charging stations are being installed within all residential complexes. To date, over 150 EV chargers have been commissioned across our projects, enabling residents an easy transition to EVs. In FY25, these chargers collectively supported approximately 3.5 million kilometres of low-emission travel.

LODHA NET ZERO URBAN ACCELERATOR

We are actively shaping the future of environmentally responsible urban development through the Lodha Net Zero Urban Accelerator, a research and development initiative in partnership with RMI India Foundation. The Accelerator focuses on decarbonisation by generating open-source research and case studies

to drive wider industry adoption and engaging stakeholders, policymakers and media to inspire broader urban transformation in India and beyond. By integrating technical innovation, strategic partnerships and impact-driven policy advocacy, the Accelerator is setting new industry standards for net-zero and environmentally responsible urban development, leading the way towards a more sustainable urban future.

UrjaAnk Urban Heat

UrjaAnk is a data-driven framework developed by the Accelerator to optimise residential energy use through real-world insights from thousands of homes in Palava, which already demonstrates a median residential energy use intensity (EUI) of approximately 40 kWh/m²/ year. By modeling consumption patterns, identifying high-impact interventions and encouraging responsible user behaviour, UrjaAnk enables better design decisions, smarter operational strategies and informed policy development. It offers a pathway to significantly reduce energy use in Indian homes while supporting economic growth and advancing national energy security.

The Accelerator is supporting Palava in pioneering heat mapping to identify urban hotspots and guide climate-responsive design. Post-development assessments show that Palava’s surface temperatures are 2-3°C lower than surrounding areas, thanks to nature-based solutions and thoughtful urban planning. By leveraging satellite data and applying urban cooling strategies, the initiative offers a replicable model for sustainable urban development, which is critical as rising urban heat emerges as a key constraint on economic productivity and public well-being for millions of Indians.

The Accelerator is actively engaging with supply chain and ecosystem stakeholders to establish a low-emission rebar steel value chain. Precast Foundation for Isolated Footings To enhance speed and consistency in foundation work, precast footings were introduced for isolated foundations. This method ensures uniform quality, reduces dependency on on-site shuttering and minimises delays due to curing or workmanship variability.

Sacrificial Wall Ties and Tie Rods in External Wall Formwork To mitigate water ingress in external walls, sacrificial wall ties and tie rods were integrated into the formwork system. These elements are designed to remain in place post-concreting, thereby reducing potential water seepage points and enhancing long-term durability.

Wind Safety Screens and Lift Shaft Platforms Prioritising worker safety, wind safety screens were installed along building peripheries, while dedicated platforms were set up at lift shaft voids. These measures ensure safe operations at heights and mitigate the risk of fall hazards in open shaft zones.

Precast Mullion Casting for Block Walls A novel approach to blockwork was achieved using precast mullions, allowing for precise alignment, better aesthetics and reduced on-site labour. This also streamlined the process of installing polished door frames and shutter with higher dimensional accuracy.

Modular Door Frame System Using FCB Subframes A modular system was developed using fibre cement board subframes to facilitate the installation of polished wooden door frames and shutters during final finishing. This prevents premature damage, eliminates re-polishing needs and ensures a seamless aesthetic.

Hybrid Formwork System – Corewall Jumpform + Aluminium Formwork For the first time, a hybrid system combining Corewall Jumpform and Aluminium Formwork was utilised to achieve monolithic casting. This integration enabled faster cycle times and superior structural integrity by reducing cold joints and enhancing alignment.

Self-Levelling Screed for Marble Flooring Replacing the traditional cement-sand bedding, a self-leveling ready-mix screed was deployed under marble flooring. This not only improved surface uniformity and bonding but also expedited laying activities while maintaining the desired finish quality.

Thermal Insulation for Terrace Slabs To improve energy efficiency, thermal insulation techniques were implemented on all terrace slabs covering habitable floors. This intervention reduces indoor heat gain, thereby enhancing occupant comfort and reducing HVAC loads.

Digital Integration of OpticVyu Cameras for Construction Site Management In line with our continued focus on technology-driven construction practices, the deployment of digital tools like the OpticVyu camera system was a key highlight this year. This initiative supports real-time site surveillance, efficient progress tracking, time-lapse documentation and improved remote collaboration; reinforcing our commitment to safety, transparency and timely delivery.

As India pursues its path towards becoming a developed nation by 2047, nurturing its brightest young minds is extremely pivotal. Despite being home to an estimated 6 million gifted students, access to high-quality gifted education programmes at scale remains a crucial challenge in our country. To bridge this gap, Lodha Foundation’s Lodha Genius Programme (LGP), in partnership with Ashoka University, has pioneered

a commitment towards identifying, nurturing and mentoring exceptionally talented students across Indian schools. This fully funded, four-week residential summer programme for grades 9-12 is followed by a year-long structured learning and personalised mentorship journey. In FY24, 195 students were selected from over 3,000 applicants, gaining access to world-class faculty, interdisciplinary courses and global opportunities. Building on this strong momentum, in FY25, LGP expanded its reach by selecting 300 gifted students from a highly competitive pool of over 7,000 applicants, ensuring that more bright young minds across India have the opportunity to realise their potential. Notably, three students from previous cohorts have already secured undergraduate admissions at world renowned institutions such as Stanford and Oxford, highlighting the programme’s role in creating pathways to global excellence and leadership for India’s future changemakers.

Ridhakshi Ganjoo, a 16-year-old student from the 2024 cohort of the LGP, is currently in Grade 11 at Government Higher Secondary School, Dadsara, located in Jammu and Kashmir. The LGP played a monumental role in shaping her academic aspirations, helping her realise that STEM can be both intellectually stimulating and socially impactful. The programme provided a nurturing ecosystem of mentors and peers, encouraging questions, curiosity and creative thinking. From conducting advanced experiments at Ashoka University, including mechanics and schlieren photography, to learning coding, lab techniques and problem solving strategies, the programme equipped Ridhakshi with valuable academic and life skills.

Ridhakshi’s pursuit of purpose and passion for creating impact

Having grown up in Pulwama, where beauty coexists with the challenges of frequent shutdowns, unreliable internet and educational disruptions, Ridhakshi deeply values the platform that the LGP has provided. It not only amplified her voice but also empowered her to transform her personal struggles into purposeful action. Today, she is committed to spreading awareness about the programme in her community, encouraging more students from conflict-affected regions to apply and benefit from the life-changing opportunities the LGP offers. Through her ongoing projects and outreach, Ridhakshi is creating a butterfly effect that continues to champion for education, creativity and resilience.

OVERVIEW OF OPERATIONS

Gross Development Value (GDV) of H ~237 Bn. Despite significant investment in growth, our balance sheet remains robust with net debt at H 39.9 Bn, 0.2x of equity, well below the target ceiling of 0.5x. The Company did not receive any financial assistance from the government during the year. During the financial year, we launched 10 new locations or new projects at existing locations. Some of the key launches during the year included Lodha Avalon, Lodha Altus, Lodha Golf View, Lodha Hanging Gardens and Lodha Opulis in MMR and Lodha Massimo and Lodha Altero in Pune. Our strategic roadmap is clearly defined to deliver predictable and robust financial performance, targeting ~20% presales growth and a healthy 20% Return on Equity (RoE), while maintaining a prudent net debt to equity ratio well below 0.5x. This ambitious yet achievable vision is underpinned by four key strategic pillars: 1. Granular growth supported by best-in-class talent and execution 2. Super-market approach to locations 3. Two phase low risk new city entry strategy and 4. Gradually building annuity income streams. To ensure robust and sustainable growth, we employ a "super market chain" approach strategically locating non-competing projects every 2-4 kilometers across our core urban markets.. This approach minimizes dependency on a particular project or location and provides steady and predictable growth in these cities, enabling us to target a significant 15-20% market share in the long term. Having entered a 'growth phase' in Bengaluru during FY25, we are now looking to replicate our super-market strategy in the city, commencing FY26 with five strategic locations, including three new project launches. Our ability to expeditiously launch projects after tying up land has made us the ‘partner of choice’ for landowners, ensuring a consistent pipeline of JDA projects. This was a significant driver enabling us to add ~ H 237 Bn in GDV in FY25. We handed over ~6,800 units to our customers. With construction in full swing, we expect significant ramp-up in deliveries in FY26.

We are a leading real estate developer in India with a strong brand presence across luxury, premium and mid-income housing segments. Our diverse portfolio includes nearly 40 operating projects across three of the largest real estate markets in India: Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR) (where we are the largest player with ~10% market share), Pune and Bengaluru. While we are primarily focussed on residential real estate development, we are also leveraging our development capability to build select annuity income streams through facilities management, industrial & warehousing (digital infrastructure) and leasing of select retail & office spaces. We have introduced ‘BelleVie’, a ditigal platform that complements our already established facilities management business, by connecting residents with a diverse range of customized marketplace services. Scaling new heights FY25 was yet another record-breaking year for the Company, with numerous indicators strengthening our conviction that the ongoing housing cycle in India is long-term and structural in nature. This shift is fuelled by the movement of the economy from low-income to mid-income, which has enhanced home buying potential for a significantly larger segment of Indian households, where the underlying aspiration has consistently been present due to both cultural and economic factors. Continuing the momentum from the previous fiscal, the Company achieved its best ever pre-sales of H 176.3 Bn (21% YoY) and best ever collections of H 144.9 Bn (29% YoY), becoming the fourth consecutive year of delivering ~20% pre-sales growth. OUR SUSTAINABILITY JOURNEY

The Board continues to maintain a strong focus on Environmental, Social and Governance (‘ESG’) priorities to ensure long-term value creation for all stakeholders through responsible and forward looking business practices. The ESG Committee plays a pivotal role in guiding this journey. The Commitee reviews and approves key ESG risks and opportunities (including climate change), sets ambitious targets and monitors our performance and external ratings in alignment with our business strategy. Our sustainability efforts this year have advanced significantly, reinforcing our leadership in decarbonising the built environment. We remain committed to achieving net-zero across our operations and developments and since March 2024, we have maintained carbon neutrality across Scope 1 and 2 emissions. Our operations continue to transition to clean energy, with renewable electricity PPAs now exceeding 10 MW across developments. Our built environment decarbonisation strategy also includes actively reducing embodied carbon in materials, deploying passive design, improving equipment efficiency, enabling clean energy access and supporting clean mobility infrastructure. We are proud to have one of the largest green-certified portfolios in the country, now exceeding 60 Mn sq ft. of certified and pre certified space. As we grow, we remain committed to standardising KPIs, tracking impact metrics and embedding sustainability at the core of our design and delivery. Our flagship Lodha Net Zero Urban Accelerator continues to act as a catalyst for innovation and collaboration in urban decarbonisation. In partnership with RMI India Foundation, we field-tested next-generation technologies such as high-efficiency air conditioners and launched the UrjaAnk initiative; India’s first of a kind residential energy behaviour experiment to uncover household electricity consumption patterns. These insights are now informing the landscape of national energy efficiency standards and contributing to India’s energy security agenda. Our pioneering efforts to mitigate urban heat, including nature-based cooling solutions demonstrated at Palava City, further exemplify our model for sustainable urbanisation. Through the Lodha Foundation, we will continue to open-source our learnings, publishing rigorous case studies and research to enable replication across India’s fast-urbanising regions. We remain proud of our continued leadership across global sustainability benchmarks. This year, we were again included in the Dow Jones Sustainability Index (DJSI) and the FTSE4Good Index and retained our position as a Global Sector Leader for residential development in the GRESB rankings. In a significant milestone, we were also recognised as the top-performing real estate company in the Urban Benchmark by the prestigious World Benchmarking Alliance.

SALIENT FEATURES OF THE NOMINATION & REMUNERATION POLICY

1. Objectives of the policy

To set out the criteria for identifying persons who are qualified to become Directors and persons who may be appointed in Senior Management and Key Managerial positions, including their remuneration.

2. Criteria for appointment of Directors, KMP and Senior Management Personnel

a. The NRC shall ascertain the integrity, qualification, expertise and experience of the person identified for appointment as Director, KMP or Senior Management and recommend his/her appointment to the Board. b. The candidate should possess impeccable reputation for integrity, deep expertise and insights in sectors / areas relevant to the Company, ability to contribute to the Company’s growth.

3. Additional criteria for proposed directors a. Should be eligible for appointment as a Director on the Board and should not be disqualified in terms of Section 164 and other applicable provisions of the Act and the Listing Regulations. b. Should have attained minimum age of 25 years. c. Should not hold directorship in more than twenty companies (including private and public limited companies) or ten public limited companies incorporated in India of which not more than seven shall be Indian listed companies. d. Should be able to devote sufficient time and efforts in discharge of duties and responsibilities effectively. e. Re-appointment/ extension of term of any Board members shall be on the basis of their performance evaluation.

4. Additional criteria for independent directors a. Should meet the baseline definition and criteria of “independence” as set out in Section 149 of the Act and the Listing Regulations.

b. Should not hold the position of Independent Director in more than seven Indian listed companies and if serving as Whole-time Director in any Indian listed company then in not more than three Indian listed companies. c. Should not hold any Board/ employment position with a competitor. The Board may in waive this requirement at its discretion.

5. Remuneration to Executive Directors a. Remuneration to Executive Directors shall be in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. b. Increments may be recommended by the NRC to the Board which should be within the limits approved by the shareholders. c. Executive Directors shall not be entitled to sitting fees for attending meetings of the Board and its committees. d. If in any three financial years during the tenure of the director, the Company has inadequate profits / losses, the Board may on the recommendation of the NRC and subject to approval of the shareholders, pay minimum remuneration to the Director in terms of Schedule V of the Act.

6. Remuneration to Independent Directors a. Independent Directors shall be entitled to a commission as may be approved by the Board in addition to sitting fees for attending Board / committee meetings. The NRC shall recommend to the Board the quantum of commission for each director based on the outcome of the evaluation process, including factors relating to attendance and time spent in the Board and committee meetings, individual contribution at meetings and contributions made by directors other than in meetings. b. The Company may pay a fair and reasonable expenditure, as may have been incurred by the director while performing his role as a director of the company, in addition to sitting fees and commission. c. Independent directors shall not be entitled to any stock options.

d. The remuneration payable shall be inclusive of any remuneration payable for services rendered by such Director in any other capacity unless the services rendered are of a professional nature and the Committee is of the opinion that the Director possesses requisite qualification for the practice of the profession. e. Where in any three financial years during the tenure of a director, the Company has inadequate profits / losses, the Board may on the recommendation of the NRC and subject to approval of the shareholders, pay remuneration to a director in terms of Schedule V of the Act.

7. Remuneration to Key managerial personnel (other than Executive Directors), Senior Management and other employees

a. The remuneration to key managerial personnel and senior management shall be sufficient to attract and retain talented and qualified individuals suitable for a role. b. Senior Management shall be assigned grades according to their qualifications, work experience

and competencies and their role and responsibility in the organisation. Individual remuneration shall be based on various factors such as job profile, skill sets, seniority, experience, performance and other benchmarking parameters. c. Remuneration to key managerial personnel shall be a balance of fixed and a performance linked variable pay component as per the company policies.. The performance linked variable pay shall be linked to individual and business performance. They shall also be entitled to annual increments which shall be reviewed and approved by the NRC annually. Additionally they may be paid / offered other benefits / perquisites, housing grants and ESOPs as per Company policies.

8. Policy implementation

The NRC is responsible for recommending the remuneration policy to the Board. The Board is responsible for approving and overseeing implementation of the remuneration policy.

CONSERVATION OF ENERGY, TECHNOLOGY ABSORPTION, FOREIGN EXCHANGE EARNINGS AND OUTGO

Particulars as required under the provisions of Section 134(3)(m) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 8 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 in respect of conservation of energy, technology absorption, foreign exchange earnings and outgo etc. are furnished below.

A. Conservation of Energy

We focus on passive design and energy efficiency to bring down the overall operational energy needs. As part of our broader sustainability agenda, we also emphasize material efficiency and the use of low-carbon materials, reducing the embodied energy of the purchased goods and materials used in building construction. 1. Steps taken or impact on conservation of energy a. Passive design measures: At the design stage, we utilize advanced simulation software such as DesignBuilder, Ansys and others to perform comprehensive analyses of ventilation, shading and thermal load. These tools help us optimize building orientation, façade design and internal layouts to enhance natural ventilation and daylight penetration while reducing unwanted heat ingress. We implement passive strategies like cross-ventilation, the stack effect and the strategic placement of windows, vents and shading elements to minimize reliance on artificial lighting and air-conditioning systems, thereby improving energy efficiency across our projects. b. Energy-efficient appliances and equipment: We deploy high-efficiency energy equipment including star rated air conditioners, LED lighting, premium efficiency motors, VVVF drive elevators, advanced parking lighting control systems. Additionally, in commercial buildings, High Coefficient of Performance (COP) Chillers, Building Management Systems (BMS) and Chiller Plant Managers (CPM) are installed to optimize HVAC operations and reduce energy consumption. c. Super-efficient air conditioning field testing: We enabled Global Cooling Efficiency Accelerator and CEPT University, in partnership with RMI to conduct a 9-month field testing of super efficient air conditioners at Palava. The study compared advanced AC prototypes—designed with superior humidity control and energy-saving features— with conventional market-available units. These

prototypes, inspired by Global Cooling Prize winning technologies, were tested in apartments with similar characteristics to ensure consistency. The testing environment presented challenging conditions, with temperatures ranging from 16.5°C to 40.8°C and humidity levels between 20.3% and 90%. We enabled this testing to help generate insights that can inform the market and policy in room air conditioners in India. d. UrjaAnk initiative: UrjaAnk is an energy conservation initiative by Lodha Foundation in collaboration with RMI India Foundation. It aims to decode residential energy usage patterns in India, set context-specific performance metrics, enable data-driven policymaking and foster energy efficient behavior through community engagement. By combining localized data with actionable insights, UrjaAnk promotes energy efficiency as a key element of sustainable urban living. e. Material efficiency and use of low-carbon materials: By prioritizing material efficiency and collaborating with our supply chain to adopt lower-carbon alternatives, we reduce the energy embedded in construction materials. For example, the use of recycled steel significantly lowers the energy required in production compared to steel produced through the blast furnace route. Similarly, increasing the use of Supplementary Cementitious Materials (SCMs) such as fly ash and Ground Granulated Blast-furnace Slag (GGBS) in concrete reduces dependence on clinker, one of the most energy-intensive components of cement, thereby cutting both embodied energy and emissions. 2. Steps Taken for utilizing alternate sources of energy a. All electricity consumed at our construction sites and commercial assets is procured exclusively from renewable sources. This includes a combination of onsite generation through third-party renewable developers, direct procurement from electricity distribution companies offering green power tariffs and open access power procurement models. Where green tariff activation is delayed due to procedural reasons, residual grid electricity is offset by purchasing Renewable Energy Certificates. We also signed a 5MWp Power Purchase Agreement to supply renewable energy to two of our commercial projects during this year.

b. We integrate renewable energy features across our developments, including solar water heating systems and rooftop photovoltaic installations. Over 5.5MW of solar power capacity has been commissioned over residential societies to offset common area electricity consumption. Additionally, more than 5 MW of cumulative solar capacity is operational across multiple buildings to power common loads. 3. Capital Investment on energy conservation equipment a. We invested approximately H 50 lakhs in the UrjaAnk initiative for procurement expert consultation services, monitoring devices and associated infrastructure to support data collection and analysis. This is a program under the Lodha Net Zero Urban Accelerator, towards which our expense is in excess of H 300 lakhs. b. We continue to invest in energy-efficient equipment such as BEE 5-star rated air conditioners, VVVF drive elevators, LED lighting, premium efficiency motors and Building Management Systems, among others. These investments amounted to approximately H48.6 crores during FY25.

B. Technology Absorption

1. Efforts made towards technology absorption We have adopted advanced simulation and analytics tools such as DesignBuilder, ANSYS and others for passive design optimization. In field operations, we have

implemented smart meters, temperature and humidity sensors and IoT-based devices to capture granular energy data. Our teams undergo continuous training to absorb emerging technologies in HVAC, lighting and material efficiency. 2. Benefits derived like product improvement, cost reduction, product development or import substitution These efforts have led to measurable improvements in building energy performance, enhanced occupant comfort, reduced operational costs and data-informed product development. Our field testing efforts have further contributed to the validation of market-ready super-efficient technologies suited to Indian climatic conditions. By advancing localized insights, we are also influencing national and state-level dialogues on urban energy efficiency. 3. Imported technology We import software tools used for design and simulation. However, the majority of construction materials and energy-efficient equipment are sourced domestically. While certain equipment components are still imported, we are witnessing a gradual shift toward local manufacturing, in line with national priorities around self-reliance and supply chain resilience.

Management Discussion

and Analysis

Review of the global economy

In CY24, despite the concerns around weak economic growth and inflationary pressures, the global economy has held steady, although the grip varies across geographies and countries. According to the International Monetary Fund, the global economy grew at 3.2% in CY24 and is expected to continue the growth momentum with growth projected at 3.3% in CY25 as well as CY26. However, that is still below the long-term average of 3.7% achieved in the first two decades of this millennium. Dark clouds of tariff tensions, primarily originating from the USA, are currently casting a shadow over the global economic landscape, creating uncertainty and potential headwinds for growth and stability. Tariffs imposed by the USA on all their trading partners coupled with counter-tariffs levied by China as well as few other countries on the USA has muddied the global growth forecasts. Failure to resolve these trade disputes swiftly could significantly impede global growth through dislocations in global trade. Led by Covid period pump-priming of the economies in various countries, inflation had been a persistent challenge throughout CY22 and CY23. In CY24, the inflation descended from its mid CY22 peak, largely due to the efforts of the central banks. Average global headline inflation fell from 6.8% in CY23 to 5.9% in CY24. It is further projected to decline to 4.2% in CY25 and 3.5% in CY26, as per IMF estimates. While on a global level, disinflation continues, there are signs of elevated inflation in a few countries. In countries where inflation remains persistently high, central banks are moving more cautiously in the easing cycle while keeping a close eye on economic activity, labour market indicators and exchange rate movements. Tariff related distortions could also raise the fear of stagflation given the impact on growth and also drive up the cost of manufactured goods. Equities in most major economies in CY25 thus far have largely mirrored the direction of trade policies emanating from the United States, particularly after the US presidential election. This policy led uncertainty in the markets is going to have an impact on the global capital flows and currencies. In general, equity valuations have become more subdued and a broad-based strengthening of the US dollar, driven primarily by expectations of higher tariffs and higher interest rates in the United States, has kept financial conditions tighter. The geopolitical landscape in CY24 remained volatile. The wars in Ukraine and in the Middle East continued to have significant impacts on global energy markets, food prices and supply chains. Brent Crude oil prices averaged US$85 per barrel in CY24, compared to US$82 in CY23, according to the International Energy Agency. Additionally, tensions between major economies like the US, China and Russia continue to influence global trade and economic stability.

Energy prices in the near future are going to remain volatile as economies grapple with tariff related uncertainties and prolonged wars in Middle East and Europe.

Review of the Indian economy

The Indian economy is projected to grow by 6.5% in FY26, which is close to the 6.4% growth seen in FY25 as well as the decadal average, but lower than the 8.2% growth that the economy clocked in FY24. The retail inflation has softened from 5.4% in FY24 to 4.9% in FY25. At the same time, the banking sector remains robust with declining asset impairments, well capitalised balance sheets and strong operational performance. As of September 2024, scheduled commercial banks demonstrated robust asset quality with Gross Non-Performing Assets falling to a 12-year low of 2.6% of gross loans and advances. Their Capital to Risk Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) stood strong at 16.7%, significantly above the norms. As a result of stable capital flows, India’s foreign exchange reserves increased from US$ 616.7 Bn at the end of January 2024 to US$ 704.9 Bn in September 2024 before moderating to US$ 676.3 Bn in March 2025. India’s forex reserves are sufficient to cover 90% of external debt and provide an import cover of nearly a year, thereby safeguarding against external vulnerabilities. Selling pressure from FPIs has led to a sharp correction in the benchmark indices and broader markets. The rupee has depreciated in line with other emerging market currencies, influenced by the US$ strengthening. The latest round of tariffs imposed by the USA, a significant trading partner for India are anticipated to negatively affect India's economic growth, largely on account of uncertainties in global trade and growth. India however is better placed than most other economies due to its large domestic economy with low dependence on exports. Additionally, Indian policy makers have been proactive in discussing a potential bilateral trade deal with the USA thus mitigating the impact of tariffs to a large extent in a shorter time frame. It also presents an opportunity for India as global manufacturers increasingly seek to diversify their sourcing away from other economies like China. Despite the challenges, India’s strong macroeconomic fundamentals and improvements in external sector indicators have helped it navigate global uncertainties. RBI expects the economy to grow around 6.5% in FY26. The union budget for FY26 has prudently balanced fiscal consolidation with growth objectives. Its emphasis on capital expenditure is complemented by measures aimed at boosting household incomes and consumption. Key indicators like higher tractor sales, rising farm incomes, increased fuel consumption, growth in air passenger traffic suggests recovery in economic momentum.

As a service driven economy with a young workforce, adoption of AI offers the potential to support economic growth and improve labour market outcomes. Prioritising education and skill development will be crucial to equipping workers with the competencies needed to thrive in an AI-augmented landscape. In May 2025, the geopolitical landscape in South Asia experienced renewed volatility due to a brief but significant military escalation between India and Pakistan. Triggered by cross-border incidents along the Line of Control and the International Border, the conflict led to a series of military responses, which, while contained diplomatically within a few weeks, marked a significant escalation in a historically volatile relationship between the two countries. The escalation resulted in short-term market disruptions. Key indices, including the Nifty 50, declined by over 4% in the immediate aftermath, accompanied by increased currency volatility. Foreign Institutional Investors reduced their exposure to Indian equities during this period, citing regional risk aversion. However, such concerns were short lived and the markets seems to have moved beyond the short- term conflict. The episode underlines the need for India to build a resilient economy, capable of withstanding external shocks and a nimble diplomatic strategy to maintain its regional and global ascent. While our Company does not have direct presence in conflict zones and our business operations remained uninterrupted, we continue to monitor regional developments closely and assess their potential second-order impacts on capital markets, consumer sentiment and investor confidence. While such conflicts introduce a layer of uncertainty, we are confident in the structural resilience of the Indian economy and its capacity to navigate short-term shocks while staying on course for long-term growth. To accelerate India's growth, the Government must prioritize a return to significant capital expenditure and increased funding for crucial infrastructure projects, while actively driving states to improve their utilization of allocated resources. The Government must continue to invest in addressing skill gaps, particularly in industry-relevant professional skills to ensure a future-ready workforce and a robust pipeline of talent.

India real estate industry overview

Despite all the external and internal roadblocks in CY24, including inflation, general elections and geopolitical tensions, India continues to be one of the fastest growing major economies in the world. The Indian real estate sector has shown robust growth since the pandemic. While initial recovery saw a surge in housing sales, commercial leasing has also gained significant traction over the past year. Hospitality sector continues to do exceedingly well with average daily rates at an all-time high. As India moves from being a low-income to a middle-income country, household incomes and spending will continue to rise giving a long runway for growth in the real estate sector. Real estate will continue being a driver of growth and employment and will continue to take larger share of the country’s GDP, as is the case in other more developed and advanced economies.

India housing market overview

A large and growing population, strong economy, high single digit wage growth and urbanization trends are expected to drive demand for housing in the years to come. There is a visible shift in customer preferences towards more branded developers, recognizing the importance of execution capability. Reforms over the last decade along with learnings from the past, for both developers as well as home buyers continue to foster a more rational and stable real estate market. As wages grow, home buyers will continue to become more discerning in their choices and will want better quality developments. Overall, the residential market across the top Indian cities is entering a phase of greater maturity, characterized by more measured growth, increased competition among branded developers and a focus on timely execution, quality of construction and affordability for the home buyer. Despite fewer launches in FY25, as compared to FY24, due to the general elections, the value of housing sales has surged from H 4.9 Tn in FY25 to H 5.7 Tn in FY25 (Source- Anarock). Due to constrained supply addition because of general elections, rising input costs and growing preference for premium housing, the prices per housing unit have escalated by a faster rate in CY24, as compared to any other year in the last 4 years. The market demonstrated improved absorption, with the inventory overhang reducing from 15 months at the close of CY23 to a healthier 14 months by the end of CY24. In developed economies, housing is a cyclical industry since over time the supply tends to overshoot the demand. As India continues on its growth path to becoming a middle-income country, the demand for housing is going to be huge, as more households become home ownership capable. The challenge will be on the supply side to scale and deliver as per the rising demand. We risk a scenario where price appreciation outstrips wage growth, eventually pushing demand to the brink. With the increasing consolidation in the housing space, organized developers wield greater power over pricing and thus bear a greater responsibility to ensure calibrated price growth. It is this combination of steady volume growth, calibrated price growth and focus on execution and timely delivery is required to ensure that housing in India remains a long-term structural play. Going forward, interest rates are projected to go down and along with the tax stimulus given to the middle class in the Union Budget, we expect an uptick in the entry level and mid-income housing, which had been severely impacted by higher interest rates in the last 3 years. FY26 looks to be promising, with demand expected to remain robust across segments.

Pune Housing Market

Similar to MMR, because of the general and state elections, Pune saw a significant gap between new launches (60,500 units) and sales (81,100 units). Inventory level has come down from 14 months to 12 months, at the end of CY24 as housing demand continues to outpace supply.

Bengaluru Housing Market

Bengaluru housing market witnessed launch and absorption of 71,000 and 65,200 units respectively in CY24. East Bengaluru accounted for 48% of new launches and 50% of absorption. Further, the share of luxury segment (H 15 Mn +) has increased to 34% in CY24 as opposed to 23% in CY23. Two primary factors have fueled this shift in demand. Firstly, Bengaluru has the most vibrant start-up ecosystem in the country, which has resulted in huge wealth creation for founders, CXOs and senior executives, the key demographic for luxury homes and secondly, a post- covid shift in general preference for larger homes and developments with more amenities for recreation and leisure. We expect these trends to continue going forward as well. As the IT sector recovers, we expect the housing demand in Bengaluru to remain robust. The city continues to lead in office leasing among the top 7 cities in India with more than 20% Grade A office stock being absorbed within the city. We anticipate development of newer micro-markets along upcoming metro corridors, particularly in North Bengaluru. As GCCs continue to prefer Bengaluru to setup and expand their existing office capacity in the country, the influx of educated talent into Bengaluru will continue and will keep rental yields higher than the other cities in the country, which in turn will fuel housing demand.

MMR Housing Market

MMR continues to be the largest market among the top 7 cities in India accounting for 32.6% of new launches and 33.8% of offtake in CY24. MMR witnessed launch of 1,34,500 housing units and absorption of 1,55,300 housing units; this divergence between offtake and new supply addition could largely be attributed to the fact that Maharashtra saw two elections in CY24. In CY24, offtake exceeded supply, resulting in a reduction of inventory levels to 14 months, down from 16 months in CY23. MMR housing will be the beneficiary of the significant infrastructure development being carried out in the city. Key infrastructure projects delivered in the last 12-15 months include, the Atal Setu (Mumbai Trans Harbour Link), Coastal Road and a few metro lines. CY25 is also going to see completion of more such large infrastructure projects such as the new airport, Mulund Airoli Palava freeway, more metro lines etc. These developments will improve city connectivity, ease capacity issues and attract more jobs, thereby boosting housing demand. Peripheral central suburbs dominated both launches and sales, taking a 25% and 26% share respectively in the total MMR market. The market share of peripheral locations is expected to increase further in the coming years, because of three factors. First, the limited availability of land and high land prices will continue to push developers to peripheral locations. Second, as connectivity improves, these peripheral locations with lower home prices, more open spaces and larger unit sizes, will appeal more to home buyers. Third, the anticipated decrease in interest rates, coupled with tax benefits, is expected to spur a surge in demand within the affordable and middle-income segments in CY25, with peripheral suburbs poised to be the primary beneficiaries of such uptick.

North Pune emerged as the most dominant zone taking a 36% share in new launches and 39% share in sales offtake in CY24. The presence of a diverse range of employers in Pune, including key industries like IT, automobiles, defence, engineered goods and manufacturing, provides the city with a broad and resilient base of potential homebuyers. This diversification ensures a more predictable housing demand, less susceptible to the cyclical ups and downs of individual sectors. With increasing wages, the nature of demand in Pune is slowly but steadily shifting to higher priced housing units. The market share of the mid segment housing (H 4 Mn to H 8 Mn) has come down from 57% in CY21 to 42% in CY24. Conversely, the high-end segment (H 8 Mn to H 15 Mn) has increased market share from 17% in CY21 to 31% in CY24. This trend is a validation of the strong economic growth prospects of the city and the increasingly discerning nature of lifestyle upgrade expected by its residents.
